concept.name: Option assignment
concept.definition: The designation by the clearing organization of an option writer who must fulfill the contract — selling the underlying at the strike (assigned call) or buying it at the strike (assigned put) — when a holder exercises.
concept.intuition: Assignment is the other side of exercise: when a holder invokes the ticket, a writer is tapped on the shoulder and must honor the deal.
concept.mechanics: When exercise notices reach the clearing organization, OCC assigns them randomly to clearing members carrying short positions in that series; members in turn allocate assignments to their customers (by random selection or first-in-first-out). Writers of American-style options can be assigned any trading day, with likelihood rising for in-the-money options near ex-dividend dates (calls) or deep in-the-money (puts).
concept.failure_modes: Writers can be assigned overnight and discover the resulting stock position only the next morning, leaving them exposed to opening gaps; assignment near ex-dividend dates can also force delivery of stock plus dividend obligations.
concept.misconceptions: Assignment is not directed at a specific writer by the exercising holder — it is allocated by the clearing organization, so no short writer can predict or prevent being selected; also, closing the short (buy to close) eliminates assignment risk only if done before assignment.
concept.example: An investor short an OICX 60 call wakes to find the call was exercised: they must sell 100 shares at $60 regardless of the current $68 market price, an immediate $8-per-share adverse fill versus the market.
